articles.text: Piedmont Cub Scouts enjoyed a wide array of scouting activities last week, including arts and crafts, STEM learning, cooking and more, at the Piedmont Council’s annual Cub Scout Day Camp. A tradition for more than 55 years, the day camp welcomes first through fifth graders for five afternoons of activities in Dracena Park. The highlight each year is the Egg Drop facilitated by the Fire Department and its 75-foot extension ladder. This year’s camp rook place from Monday-Friday, June 9-13. Each day the campers cycled through six stations – crafts, Den time, Scout skills, sports, STEM activities, and cooking. Each station showed unique daily activities inspired by this year’s camp theme, “Invention Convention.” The crafts station had Cubs making a rubber band-powered rocket out of a pool noodle, as Cub Scouts in the Purple Den raise the flag to start off the last day of camp. As the community of followers of Jesus experienced the love of God, the grace of Jesus and the strength of the Holy Spirit it came to understand that Trinity described their experience. articles.text: Editor: When the City of Piedmont considered developing new sports fields in Blair Park from 2008 to 2012, there were years of studies, a lawsuit and much controversy. Neighbors and I attended meetings and read reports where experts and citizens explained why development was too dangerous, even with a pedestrian bridge and/or a crosswalk and/ or a traffic light to have persons crossing busy Moraga Ave by Coaches field. Inadequate sightlines were a big part of that calculation. Identified safety issues weren’t limited to the Coaches field site but also linked to challenges farther up the hill looking at traffic impacts and projected dangers of bottlenecks all along Moraga Avenue which serves as an important emergency escape route for both Piedmont and Oakland residents. An environmental impact study in 2010 found that stopping sight distances for the former development plan did not meet Caltrans safety standards. What has changed in 15 years to make Moraga Canyon a safe location for major development? I attended the April 30 presentation by project consultants where traffic issues related to proposed Moraga Canyon development were discussed. The consultant acknowledged traffic sightlines are a continuing concern yet was dismissive of projected impacts, saying they would be quite minimal. The report did not address any impacts along the length of Moraga Avenue outside the boundaries of Piedmont, even knowing how close Highway 13 is to the border and the challenges of the intersection at Harbord Drive. I appreciate the thoughtful questions to the consultants I observed at the Council meeting on April 30, though there were few people in attendance to hear. Development of Moraga Canyon was not deemed safe in 2010 or 2012. Please continue to question how it can be safer now with more density and traffic. This could be a life-or-death decision.

articles.text: Editor: Recently, several parents shared their heartfelt concerns about changes to our elementary instrumental music program in a letter to the editor. Their passion for music education is admirable and reflects our community’s deep commitment to the arts. After reviewing the district’s plan, I’d like to share an alternative viewpoint. I believe these changes represent an exciting opportunity to strengthen our performing arts program. The district is thoughtfully reimagining elementary performing arts to provide more diverse opportunities for our students beyond instrumental music. They’ll be evaluating this new approach alongside existing programs in visual arts, technology, and library, with the goal of also introducing world language in 5th grade the following year. Here’s what’s actually happening next year: 4th graders will receive 60 minutes of theater arts weekly (replacing the current 40-minute instrumental music class), while 5th graders receive a full 60 minutes of dedicated instrumental music instruction. Previously, students received 40 minutes of instrumental music in both 4th and 5th grades (80 minutes total). Now they’ll receive 60 minutes in each grade—120 minutes total across their elementary years. That’s a 50% increase in performing arts instruction! Additionally, instrumental music class sizes will be cut in half with increased staffing, allowing for more individualized attention and meaningful instruction time. As the parent of a recent 4th grade instrumental music student most of the instructional period was spent on logistics rather than actual playing and learning. Theater arts will provide tremendous benefits, including building confidence, empathy, creativity, and collaboration skills—all backed by extensive research which was cited by the district in their evaluation. By introducing theater in 4th grade while strengthening instrumental music in 5th grade, we’re helping more children discover their unique talents and passions in the performing arts. The district spent months developing this proposal through a collaborative process involving teachers, administrators, and performing arts staff. While change can feel uncomfortable, our administration has demonstrated remarkable success in improving programs, increasing enrollment, and enhancing communication across the district. They’ve found a way to consistently give parents and students more of what they want and need while communicating about it transparently. I encourage our community to embrace a new approach that seeks to expand opportunities for all our students. Let’s support our district as they work to create a more comprehensive and inclusive performing arts education for every child. Sincerely, Adam Fishman Dad to a rising 5th grader (WW) and 7th grader (PMS)

articles.text: Piedmont’s upcoming Shell Electric Vehicle (EV) Charging Station at 29 Wildwood Avenue has issued a notice of Environmental Assessment Activities to neighbors. Work on additional environmental investigation at the site of the former Shell service station was scheduled to begin on Tuesday, June 17, with samples being retrieved on July 1. According to the notice, the work will examine the extent of contamination in the property’s soil vapor, or air spaces between particles of soil. Four soil vapor sampling devices will be buried three feet deep along the northern property boundary and near the former tank areas where chlorinated solvents have previously been detected. The samples will be retrieved on July 1 and submitted to a lab for analysis. The work, overseen by Alameda County Environmental Health Department (ACEHD), will take place from 8:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. each day and activities include use of a handheld drill and a support vehicle. Dust and odors are expected to be controlled, but the notice encourages any concerns to be directed immediately to Tracy Craig at (510) 334-4866. Once this work is complete, the site will be secured until approval is given for abatement of lead/ asbestos and demolition of the existing building. articles.text: Workers prepare to lift the backup generator into place with a crane. A backup generator and Motor Control Center electrical panel for Piedmont’s new 911 Dispatch Center arrived and were put into place using a crane on Monday, June 9. The generator and the electrical panel are items listed as “critical path” on the construction schedule, and their installation marks a milestone on the completion schedule for the Dispatch Center. This equipment serves as an independent and secure power source to continue operations during outages and challenging conditions. Piedmont’s Dispatch Center will be located in the former Emergency Operations Center and the Police Department conference room. The Dispatch Center functions as the “nerve center” for the Piedmont public safety services, fielding over 13,000 calls annually for the Police and Fire Departments. According to the City, the former space was severely undersized, unable to accommodate modern technologies, and located in an area that has not been seismically retrofitted. Concurrent with the building improvements, the City recently increased dispatch staffing for the first time since 1978. Renovation of the dispatch center was identified by the City Council as the highest and best use for American Rescue Plan Act funding in October 2021. Design work for the relocated dispatch center began in 2022, and the City Council awarded a $1.8 million construction contract for the project in March of 2023. Construction began in June 2024. articles.text: Every summer, Piedmont’s population diminishes significantly as soon as the final school bells signal the arrival of summer vacation. The most popular and time-honored migration from Piedmont is to Camp Augusta in Nevada City. On Saturday, June 8, two large buses picked up campers at Piedmont Park and headed to camp on the shores of Lake Vera. Camp Augusta was donated to the girls of Piedmont in 1931 by Edwin William Ehmann and Charlotte Ehmann. For at least the last 80 years, the site has operated as a summer camp and provided a favorite home away from home, for tens of thousands of Piedmont kids and any interested kids aged 8-16, regardless of city origin. Camp Augusta’s success is unrivaled. It has been fully booked since 2009. The camp provides more than the beauty of a Sierra Nevada forest; youth receive the opportunity to try out and explore hundreds of new activities, skills and passions, like swimming, horseback riding, canoeing, and rock climbing. The first session of camp began last week. Each weekend of the summer the buses will be back in town, returning satiated campers and collecting new busloads of kids heading to a wonderland called Camp Augusta. A line down Highland Avenue forms as parents say goodbye to their kids headed to the first session of Camp Augusta. Families wait in line to load their kids and camp gear onto buses headed for Camp Augusta.

Ken, a board member of Piedmont Makers since 2018, has played many important roles. He served on the Advisory Committee for the Mary G. Ross Engineering Lab, was a Mechanical Mentor for Highlander Robotics, and was Commissioner for FIRST Tech Challenge. Vaughn, the outgoing captain of Highlander Robotics, has been a dedicated participant in FIRST Robotics through Piedmont Makers for seven years. Over his four years as driver for Highlander Robotics, he led the team to four consecutive appearances at the FIRST World Championship – including a run as Division Finalist – while being a familiar face at both the Piedmont School Maker Fairs and the East Bay Mini Maker Fair. Together, they’ve built everything from t-shirt slingshots to rocket launchers, enriching our community with their creative spirit. This year, they have outdone themselves: over six months, Vaughn and Ken designed and led the fabrication of a 27’×54’ welded steel and polycarbonate field perimeter needed for FIRST Robotics Competition events. They secured more than $30,000 in in-kind donations from material suppliers and coordinated a team of 35 volunteers, who together logged over 1,000 hours building the new practice field infrastructure. Today, the field stands as a vital resource for 19 regional teams who have spent countless hours there refining their robots. They were thanked for their dedication to improving our community. Vaughn will be a freshman at MIT this fall.

It’s off to Camp Augusta – by the busload By Jay Russell Every summer, Piedmont’s population diminishes significantly as soon as the final school bells signal the arrival of summer vacation. The most popular and time-honored migration from Piedmont is to Camp Augusta in Nevada City. On Saturday, June 8, two large buses picked up campers at Piedmont Park and headed to camp on the shores of Lake Vera. Camp Augusta was donated to the girls of Piedmont in 1931 by Edwin William Ehmann and Charlotte Ehmann. For at least the last 80 years, the site has operated as a summer camp and provided a favorite home away from home, for tens of thousands of Piedmont kids and any interested kids aged 8-16, regardless of city origin. Camp Augusta’s success is unrivaled. It has been fully booked since 2009. The camp provides more than the beauty of a Sierra Nevada forest; youth receive the opportunity to try out and explore hundreds of new activities, skills and passions, like swimming, horseback riding, canoeing, and rock climbing. The first session of camp began last week. Each weekend of the summer the buses will be back in town, returning satiated campers and collecting new busloads of kids heading to a wonderland called Camp Augusta. A line down Highland Avenue forms as parents say goodbye to their kids headed to the first session of Camp Augusta. articles.text: Do you ever just look down and wonder, when on earth did the floor get so far away? Or, realize that you’ve somehow grown into the huge shirt your parents bought you “for the future” — and now, “the future” is…now?? Or, personally, I get the feeling that Witter Field’s looking smaller every PE class, but somehow expands again when we’re told its mile day. All of these are reminders that time is ticking…. And now: Boom, it’s the last Wednesday of middle school. Like, ever. In retrospect, it’s been quite the rollercoaster ride. Maybe for you it’s been getting to know yourself or others better, discovering new passions, or trying (and failing) to cut down that 7 hour screentime. Maybe you’re just mourning the tragic fact you aged out of the“kids eat free” IHOP deal. Whatever steps we’ve taken on this journey, middle school has definitely had its share of ups, downs, and everything in between. After all, it hasn’t just been having real homework and somehow getting used to not having recess — it’s been a period of self exploration. And we can’t forget the cheerleaders that have been with us every leap, wobble, and step of the way. To our teachers, staff, parents and everyone who has been part of this wild ride — thank you for all of the Sophia Li delivering her student speech for Piedmont Middle School’s 8th grade graduation. kindness you have shown us. People love to compare life to a lot of things: a road, a game, a play. But for me, I’ve always thought life is most like writing a book. You can write pretty much anything you want to, but every new chapter builds on the ones from before. Especially going through middle school, the journey of self-discovery is also one that’s shaped by who you currently are, who you want to be, and the steps you take to get there. And here’s what I’ve learned: you don’t need to do what everyone else is doing in order to be at the top of your game. If everyone’s emptying their wallets on Jellycats and Lululemon, and that’s your cup of tea, go for it. But if it isn’t, don’t sweat it. However cliche it sounds, a one-size-fitsall for humanity doesn’t exist and it’s a good thing that it never will. Taylor Swift once said, “I promise that you’ll never find another like me.” Turns out, she’s right. You are your own greatest strength. So, as we close the chapter of middle school, let’s not be afraid to throw ourselves out there. Take that hard class. Join that club. Spend time on the things you enjoy. I can’t wait to write the next chapter with you all and embrace whatever high school throws at us. So, to my fellow middle school graduates, cheers to the bright road ahead! • Inclusion, and Belonging Council. Someone who always shows up to help people with her whole being. Also, Tommy Ashton, whom I frequently see down at the weight room putting in the extra mile in strength and mobility training, who always shows up as his best on the field, even when his only audience was my weight room class, most of whom were barely making it through their mandatory PE credits. These are just a few of many examples of my exceptional classmates who portray what it is that makes humanity so lovely. What makes people dynamic and compelling is the ability to find passion and live it out in full, unapologetically, with chalance. So what does this mean for us, going forward? It means going into the rest of our lives that we can’t be afraid to experiment, innovate, exist loudly: take that 101 class you’re not sure you’ll like, join that intramural team, apply for the internship, talk to that girl at the cafe or the football game. Take a chance on life. The fear of being perceived as alive and invested should never stop you from exploring, rather showing those around just how alive and invested you are is what makes you powerful. So I want to extend a thank you to all our teachers, classmates, families, administrators, and everyone who has shown us the power of a full life. We are the class of 2025, and if we let ourselves live fully, there’s no telling what we can accomplish, what legacies we can make ring, because human potential isn’t in the moments of nonchalance and deflection, but in the times we let ourselves find connection through our passion, let ourselves be seen, and let ourselves be unapologetically chalant.

articles.text: A small crowd filled the Piedmont Unified School District Wellness Center on Thursday, May 29, to honor Piedmont High School counselor Amanda Carlson as winner of the Brooke Zimmerman Award. Carlson was given the award for her outstanding service to Piedmont students and her partnership with the Wellness Center, the district’s hub for student mental health support. The Brooke Zimmerman plaque stands as a testament to the counselors, staff and volunteers who show up for Piedmont students every day. Wellness Center co-founder and former Piedmont Middle School Counselor Brooke Zimmerman attended the celebration with her grandson, Cy Leonard, a recent fifth-grade graduate of Beach Elementary. Zimmerman and a small committee founded the Center in 2007 to address rising student stress and anxiety levels. Today, the Wellness Center has become a regional model, inspiring schools such as Castro Valley High School to open wellness centers based on Piedmont’s example. Superintendent Dr. Jennifer Hawn and Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich also joined the ceremony in affirmation of PUSD’s dedication to student well-being. “We are committed to supporting the Wellness Center as a thriving part of our school programs,” said Hawn. Millennium High School Principal Irma Muñoz Daniels opened the awards ceremony by reminding attendees why the Center’s mission matters. “The work of supporting student mental health is not just important – it is essential,” she said. The Wellness Center, located behind the library at Piedmont High School, provides free mental health services to Piedmont Middle, High and Millennium students. After finishing her sophomore year at Piedmont High School, Brynne Jones will study Mandarin this summer in Taiwan on a National Security Language Initiative for Youth (NSLI‑Y) scholarship. Jones was one of 440 students selected from thousands of high school applicants across the United States to receive a scholarship. While in Taiwan, Jones will live with a host family and engage with local peers to enhance language learning. The program will last around seven weeks, and participants receive a minimum of 120 hours of classroom instruction in intensive language classes. “To prepare, I’ve been using Duolingo, especially for speaking, and watching Chinese movies to practice my Mandarin. The program also had several virtual information sessions to help us prepare, which have been super helpful,” said Jones. Jones visited China with six students and Piedmont Mandarin teacher Xinjia Xia during Spring Break in early April, giving her valuable experience about living in there. The rich culture in Taiwan captured her interest to study abroad this summer, especially the lively night markets, great street food and seeing local temples. “I’m most excited to meet my host family and experience everyday life in Taiwan,” said Jones. The program is part of the U.S. Department of State’s Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs, which promotes the study of Chinese (Mandarin), Hindi, Indonesian, Korean, Persian (Tajiki), Russian, Turkish, and Arabic. Launched in 2006 as part of a multi-agency U.S. Government initiative, the program increases the number of young Americans with the critical language skills necessary to contribute to U.S national security and economic competitiveness. Many program alumni go on to pursue education and careers vital to the U.S. NSLI‑Y is administered by American Councils for International Education in cooperation with AFS‑USA, American Cultural Exchange Service, Amideast, iEARN‑USA, Stony Brook University, and the University of Delaware. Applications for NSLI‑Y programs are available at Nsliforyouth.org each fall. The U.S. Department of State provides additional study abroad opportunities for both American and international high school students. Americans can welcome a new language and culture into their home by hosting an international exchange student, which is a life-changing experience for students, host families, schools, and communities. Visit Exchanges.state.gov and Hosting. state.gov for more.

The event was billed as a kids’ dance party, as the Beach Revue Band played summer classics for a crowd of several hundred partygoers. By Jay Russell After finishing her sophomore year at Piedmont High School, Brynne Jones will study Mandarin this summer in Taiwan on a National Security Language Initiative for Youth (NSLI‑Y) scholarship. Jones was one of 440 students selected from thousands of high school applicants across the United States to receive a scholarship. While in Taiwan, Jones will live with a host family and engage with local peers to enhance language learning. The program will last around seven weeks, and participants receive a minimum of 120 hours of classroom instruction in intensive language classes. “To prepare, I’ve been using Duolingo, especially for speaking, and watching Chinese movies to practice my Mandarin. The program also had several virtual information sessions to help us prepare, which have been super helpful,” said Jones. Jones visited China with six students and Piedmont Mandarin teacher Xinjia Xia during Spring Break in early April, giving her valuable experience about living in there. The rich culture in Taiwan captured her interest to study abroad this summer, especially the lively night markets, great street food and seeing local temples. “I’m most excited to meet my host family and experience everyday life in Taiwan,” said Jones. The program is part of the U.S. Department of State’s Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs, which promotes the study of Chinese (Mandarin), Hindi, Indonesian, Korean, Persian (Tajiki), Russian, Turkish, and Arabic. Launched in 2006 as part of a multi-agency U.S. Government initiative, the program increases the number of young Americans with the critical language skills necessary to contribute to U.S national security and economic competitiveness. Many program alumni go on to pursue education and careers vital to the U.S. NSLI‑Y is administered by American Councils for International Education in cooperation with AFS‑USA, American Cultural Exchange Service, Amideast, iEARN‑USA, Stony Brook University, and the University of Delaware. Applications for NSLI‑Y programs are available at Nsliforyouth.org each fall. The U.S. Department of State provides additional study abroad opportunities for both American and international high school students. Americans can welcome a new language and culture into their home by hosting an international exchange student, which is a life-changing experience for students, host families, schools, and communities. Visit Exchanges.state.gov and Hosting. state.gov for more. articles.text: The full-sized model of the Mercury capsule at the Chabot Space & Science Center We are living through a space renaissance: an era defined by groundbreaking innovation, historic achievements, and big questions about our future. What’s remarkable about this moment in time is that it isn’t limited to distant launchpads or orbiting satellites. The space renaissance is unfolding right here on Earth, in labs, classrooms, studios, and observatories—including right here in the Bay Area. Silicon Valley startups are developing next-generation satellites and NASA Ames is helping develop the Vented Fly Box, a specialized research chamber used aboard the International Space Station to study DNA repair in fruit flies (tiny organisms whose genetic similarities to humans make them powerful models for understanding the impacts of space travel on human health). Our region is at the center of this exciting new chapter in space exploration and Chabot Space & Science Center, a longtime hub for science, technology, engineering, art, and math (STEAM) education, is proud to be part of this movement. The technologies developed for space exploration are already enhancing life on Earth in remarkable ways. NASA Aqua and Terra satellites have collected years of data on wildfire behavior, allowing scientists to potentially improve the future of wildfire management. The camera in your smartphone? It exists because of NASA research into compact imaging systems. These examples, and so many more, show how pushing the boundaries of what’s possible in space leads to practical solutions at home. But innovation flows in both directions. Artists, designers, and creators on Earth are influencing how we explore the universe. Origami-inspired folding techniques have been used to design reduced size and weight antennas and solar arrays, which are not only space-saving, but less costly to boot. This interplay between art and science is one of the defining features of the space renaissance. Chabot Space & Science Center believes that everyone (a curious kid, a seasoned engineer, or someone who simply loves to look up at the stars and be in nature) has a place in this story. Space Week, a new event that celebrates the future of space exploration and the communities shaping it, takes place July 30th through August 3rd. Through hands-on activities, live science demonstrations, telescope viewings, conversations with experts, NASA and more, we’ll connect people of all ages to the innovations and ideas transforming our understanding of the universe and our place in it. Space Week is more than a celebration. It’s an invitation to see yourself as part of this moment in history. The decisions we make and the technologies we develop today will shape the future of life on Earth and beyond. Chabot Space & Science Center is here to spark curiosity, inspire discovery, and support the next generation of explorers. The 2024-25 school year is has officially concluded at Piedmont High with teams turning the page on another sports calendar. In this article, the Post reflects on our favorite moments from the recent sports seasons. 1. Boys’ Soccer’ wins CIF NorCal Championship As the No. 5 seed in the Division 5 CIF NorCal tournament, Piedmont High’s boys’ soccer team battled its way to claim the title. They opened with a 1-nil upset over No. 4 Orland and also kept a clean sheet in the semifinals in a 2-nil win over No. 8 Colusa. Then in the Final, Piedmont defeated No. 7 Williams 4-1 for the championship including a first-half hat trick by Gianluca Bini and Bosco Lorin scoring Piedmont’s final goal. 2. Girls’ Basketball’s competes in Open Div. in State Tourney The girls’ basketball team received the No. 5 seed in the NCS Open Division, which is considered the top echelon of the section with a batch of freshmen like Andrea Martin, Jenelle Solis, and Savannah Dennig, and sophomore Taylor White. They lost 51-45 to No. 4 Cardinal Newman in the opening round but won 70-48 over No. 6 Salesian in the fifth-place final. They received the No. 9 seed in the Division 1 CIF State Tournament, dominating No. 8 Oakland Tech 60-29 in the first round and won 62-60 over No. 16 San Joaquin Memorial at Binks Rawlings Gym. They lost to No. 4 St. Mary’s of Stockton 61-48 in the regional semifinals. 3. Sebastien Swain in 2 State Championships Sophomore distance runner Sebastien Swain was one of our honorable mention for Athlete of the Year recipients after his monumental 2024-campaign. In the spring track season, Swain ran his way to the 2025 CIF State Track and Field Championship in Clovis, where he placed 18th of 29 runners in the 800 in 1:53.15. Back in the fall for cross country, he finished 96th of 201 in the 2024 CIF State Cross Country Championship at Woodward Park. 4. Sophomores at State Cross Country Championship Along with Swain reaching the CIF State Cross Country Championship, Piedmont also sent two sophomores from the girls’ team: Leighton Mand and Amalia Gray. Mand finished the race in 74th of 201 runners with a time of 19:52.7 on the 5,000 meter course, while Gray placed 101st in 20:24.5. We named Mand this year’s Sophomore of the Year. 5. Miguel Long wins Del Campo Decathlon & Stanford Invitational Miguel Long won our 2025 Athlete of the Year thanks in part to a monumental run in April. On April 5, Long won the prestigious Stanford Invitational by reaching 45 feet, 8.5 inches—marking his personal record while in a field of 18 athletes. Then on April 18-19, he won the Del Campo Decathlon with a score of 5,369 points in a field of 19. He finished in the top-10 of every event, including winning the long jump in 21 feet, 3 inches, the high jump in 6 feet, 7.5 inches, and the 110 meter hurdles in 16.69 seconds. 6. Nia Kim’s breakout season Nia Kim was also our 2025 Athlete of the Year after her breakout year on track and field. She became a WACC champion on May 7 in the 100 meter hurStaff Photos dles with a time of 15.62 seconds and won the NCS Bayshore Area title in 15.19 on May 17. Nia also placed second of 15 at the WACC Championship in the high jump with a height of five feet. She jumped the same height at the NCS Bayshore Area Championship to place third of 18. Her 4x400 team placed second of 14 at the Bayshore in 4:09.20. 7. PHS swim team’s lights-out relay team Piedmont’s boys’ swim team became the first team in school history to send two relay teams to the CIF State Championship: Owen Blanford, Cole Carnazzo, Nik Costello, Dima Secor, and Asher Takazawa. Both the 200 and 400 freestyle teams won the WACC Championship, clocking respective times of 1:34.27 and 3:11.09. Then at the NCS Championship, the 200 team was fifth of 16 in 1:33.24, while the 400 team was seventh of 16 in 3:07.68. At State, the 200 medley relay team posted a time of 1:33.84, finishing 23rd out of 40 teams. Secor replaced Costello in the 400 freestyle relay, finishing 21st of 40 in 3:07.38. 8. Girls’ Lacrosse loses NCS in overtime The girls team battled to the D2 NCS Championship as the No. 6 seed before losing to No. 4 College Park 8-7 in sudden death overtime for the title. This year marked Piedmont’s first NCS semifinals and finals appearance since winning the 2019 title. To reach the finals, Piedmont obliterated No. 11 Cardinal Newman 16-3 in the first round, upset No. 3 Lick-Wilmerding 5-4 in the quarterfinals, and dominated arch-rivals No. 2 Bishop O’Dowd 16-8 in the semifinals. 9. Boys’ Basketball team in near comeback in NCS Championship The Highlanders went 15-16 and reached the D4 NCS Finals as the No. 1 seed before losing No. 11 St. Patrick 75-70. To get there, PHS beat No. 16 Ukiah 87-49 in the first round, No. 9 Bethel 78-69 in the quarterfinals and No. 12 Windsor 60-53 in the semifinals. They qualified for the D4 CIF State tournament as the No. 9 seed, losing to No. 8 Natomas 84-71. Staff Photos Sebastien Swain competed at the State meet in both cross-country and track. articles.text: Audrey Lam is a Piedmont High graduate from the Class of 2023 and was the Post’s Honorable Mention for Athlete of the Year as a senior. Lam just finished her sophomore year at Brown University and is currently playing locally with Oakland Soul’s pre-professional W League team. Lam recently logged her first assist with Soul in the club’s 2-1 loss to Stockton Cargo on June 7 while playing in front of thousands of spectators at the Oakland Coliseum. The W League is considered one of the top semi-professional leagues in the country, often featuring players who are competing in other Division 1 colleges or are on the fringe of top leagues around the world. Playing alongside Lam includes former Stanford national champion Sam Tran, former Thailand National Team forward Miranda Nild, and fringe NWSL talent Shaelan Murison, who got time with the Utah Royals. “Everyone at Brown is asked to play in the summer to prepare for the fall season. I was looking at all my options and tried to determine what would be a high-performance team and give me good competition. It’s been a great experience; all these players are really great,” said Lam. “The coaching staff and everyone at Soul has been amazing.” With Soul, Lam received four straight starts as a central midfielder, proving her playmaking ability. She takes almost all of the team’s free kicks and corners. “Audrey had a short stint with us last year and it’s great to have her back,” said Soul head coach Jessica Clinton. “You really see what she brings to the game. The goal is to see what our core players look like going forward and Audrey Lam had an assist for Oakland Soul at the Oakland Coliseum on June 7. Audrey certainly can be that,” Appearing earlier with Oakland Soul was Piedmont grad Aubrey Turner (Class of 2020). She finished her collegiate career at the University of Portland and played for F.C. Famalicão in the top tier of Portuguese football in 2024. “It’s great to play with Aubrey,” said Lam. “I haven’t seen her in a while so it was great to see her with Soul. In 2023 as a freshman, Audrey helped Brown go 12-2-3 and earn the No. 3 seed in its bracket for the 2023 NCAA Tournament. They beat Quinnipiac 3-nil in the first round, but lost to No. 6 Mississippi State 2-1 in the second round. Lam elected to take the following year off, but is looking to remerge on Brown’s lineup come the fall. “I made a difficult decision. articles.text: Here is the Gold Cup’s 2025 bracket. Who do you have winning it? Summer soccer is here! The CONCACAF Gold Cup has already returned over the past week with the United States opening with a 5-nil shellacking of Trinidad and Tobago on Sunday, June 15 to open Group D’s action. FIFA rankings are shown for each team, and our final predictions of how the tournament plays out. We’ll start with the United States’ Group C and go from there. Group D: No. 16 USA, No. 58 Saudi Arabia, No. 83 Haiti, No. 100 Trinidad and Tobago The United States has caught some flak for missing some of their top talent for the Gold Cup, including AC Milan’s Christian Pulisic. Juventus’ Weston McKennie and Tim Weah are unavailable because of the FIFA Club World Cup. Despite being without several of their best players, this should be an easy qualification into the knockout stages. No. 100 Trinidad and Tobago clearly didn’t post much of a problem for the Stars and Stripes. Haiti opened the tournament with a 1-nil loss to Saudi Arabia, which looks like the U.S.A.’s biggest threat in the group. I’m taking USA to win the group and Saudia Arabia to take the second spot. USA and Saudi Arabia play on Thursday, while the U.S. Men’s national team closes the group stage against Haiti on June 22. Group A: No. 17 Mexico, No. 54 Costa Rica, No. 137 Suriname, No. 139 Dominican Republic Mexico walks into the tournament arguably with the best 26-man roster, including West Ham midfielder Edson Álvarez, AC Milan forward Santiago Gimenez, and Fulham striker Raul Jiménez. Although they looked lackluster against Dominican Republic in a 3-2 win on June 14, I’m still taking El tri as 1A. Costa Rica had a high-scoring affair against Suriname in a surprising 4-3 shootout. Costa Rica still looked like a high-powered bunch with 19 shots, so I’m not taking any surprises; Costa Rica as 2A. Davies, they’ll still be led by Lille striker Jonathan David. I’m taking them to win the group. Picking the second team gets a bit more difficult. Honduras played Canada on Tuesday, along with Curacao and El Salvador. Honduras against El Salvador on June 21 will likely determine the fate. Honduras comes into the tournament on three straight wins, so I’m taking them as 2B. Group C: No. 33 Panama, No. 63 Jamaica, No. 106 Guatemala, Unranked Guadeloupe Guatemala pulled off a pretty shocking 1-nil upset of Jamaica on June 16, putting the Reggae Boyz in danger of getting knocked out. Panama got the job done with a 5-2 whooping of Guadeloupe, so I’m taking them as 1C. The question is whether Jamaica can recover. I’m thinking Guatemala pulls it off and gets out the group. Costa Rica has talented athletes playing in Europe, and I’m thinking they are good enough to beat a shaken United States program. Semifinals Canada beats Costa Rica; Mexico beats Panama. I like Canada. Jesse Marsch’s bunch beat the United States 2-1 back in March and I think Jonathan David is good enough to lead them past Costa Rica. As for Mexico, I stand by my words that they have the best roster of the tournament. Finals Mexico defeats Canada. articles.text: Wayne Thiebaud: Art Comes from Art, the first exhibition to highlight Thiebaud’s extensive reinterpretations of works by his artistic heroes, is on display at the Legion of Honor in San Francisco now through August. Thiebaud was an American painter known for his colorful works depicting commonplace objects like pies, pastries, and hot dogs, most often associated with the Pop art movement because of his interest in objects of mass culture. Wayne Thiebaud: Art Comes from Art is the first exhibition to spotlight his extensive involvement with art history throughout his six-decade-long career until his death in 2021. The exhibition is a facet of the “Legion of Honor 100,” a yearlong centennial celebration of San Francisco’s fine arts museums and its collections. The exhibition includes 65 pieces by Thiebaud, representing his wide-ranging reinterpretations of old and new European and American artworks spanning the years 1957 to 2020. “As a self-identified ‘thief,’ who mined the work of his predecessors and contemporaries, Wayne Thiebaud’s practice was deeply rooted in his study of art history, but this aspect of his work has never been explored,” said Thomas P. Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “Over the course of the next year, as we reflect upon the Legion of Honor’s legacy as a center of art historical research and inspiration, Wayne Thiebaud: Art Comes from Art couldn’t be more timely.” Exhibition curator Timothy Anglin Burgard said Thiebaud’s engagement with art history at large “revealed his belief that the world of art transcended limiting definitions of time and place, as well as progress. Viewed from this perspective, the entire global history of art, encompassing every movement and style, was as accessible, relevant, and inspiring to Thiebaud as contemporary art,” he said. articles.text: Festival Napa Valley’s 2025 summer season kicks off July 5 at outdoor venues and popular wineries throughout Napa Valley, including Charles Krug Winery in St. Helena and Nickel & Nickel in Oakville. The festival, now in its 19th season, is presented annually by the nonprofit Napa Valley Festival Association, governed by a board of vintners and local business owners. The festival spans the Napa Valley region and presents performances at many wineries that are rarely open to the public. Taste of Napa, a signature event within the summer festival, showcases wine and culinary delicacies from approximately 80 local wineries, restaurants and food artisans. Festival Napa Valley also presents year-round school programming and is the leading private funder of arts education in Napa County public schools, offering programs for students, tuition-free academies for young emerging artists and scholarships for students studying music. This year, Festival Napa Valley is also introducing a “Choose Your Price” ticket model for select concerts during the 2025 summer season, allowing attendees to choose ticket prices starting as low as free to $5, with the option of contributing more. Festival Napa Valley runs from July 5 to 20. Visit https://festivalnapavalley.org for the full summer lineup and to purchase tickets. articles.text: Play ends June 21 San Francisco Playhouse’s production The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time, based on the novel by Mark Haddon and adapted by Simon Stephens, is playing onstage now through June 21. Haddon’s 2003 mystery novel has been critically acclaimed for its portrayal of neurodivergence, featuring a main character who is described as a “bright mathematician with behavioral problems.” The novel is narrated by 15-yearold Christopher John Francis Boone and chronicles his investigation into the murder of his neighbor’s dog. The book won the Whitbread Book Awards for Best Novel and Book of the Year, the Commonwealth Writers’ Prize for Best First Book, and the Guardian Children’s Fiction Prize. Brendan Looney makes his San Francisco Playhouse debut as protagonist Christopher, who discovers his neighbor’s dog dead, stabbed by a kitchen fork, and launches his own guerrilla investigation. Christopher is determined to solve the mystery of who murdered Wellington and carefully records each fact of the crime. But his detective work, forbidden by his father, takes him on a thrilling journey that upturns his world. Mark P. Robinson also makes his Playhouse debut as Ed Boone, Christopher’s father. Cassidy Brown, Laura Domingo, Whit K. Lee, Catherine Luedtke, Renee Rogoff, and Wiley Naman Strasser round out the ensemble. San Francisco Playhouse Producing Director and co-founder Susi Damilano leads the production with movement direction by Bridgette Loriaux. The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time is playing onstage through June 21 at San Francisco Playhouse 450, Post Street. For tickets and more information, visit sfplayhouse.org or call the box office at 415-677- 9596. Photo by Jessica Palopoli Mark P. articles.text: Marah Sotelo (Maria) and Lucy Fisch as Liesl, Jaxon Hunt as Friedrich, Miranda Klein as Louisa, Ray Khalili as Kurt, Sage Luu as Brigitta, Kaylee Lopez as Marta, Erin Koh as Gretl in Berkeley Playhouse’s production of The Sound of Music Berkeley Playhouse closes its current season with The Sound of Music, playing onstage now through June 29. The musical, based on the 1949 memoir The Story of the Trapp Family Singers, premiered years before the widely-popular 1965 American musical film. Berkeley Playhouse director Danny Cozart said the beloved, timeless musical is one of his all-time favorites that “continues to become more relevant day by day.” “The themes we are looking to explore in this production are the choices a person must make when the different structures of society [including] family, religion, and the state, are imposing conflicting demands on them.” Cozart said. “Our focus for this production is to drive home the real-world consequences of political action and the impact on a family trying to stay together in the face of looming tyranny.” The cast includes Marah Sotelo as Maria Rainer, Teressa Foss as Mother Abbess, Chloe Angst as Sister Berthe, Sage Alberto as Sister Margaretta, Akshaya Lakshmi as Sister Sophia, Robert Lopez as Captain Georg Von Trapp and Phillip Leyva as Franz. A cast of young musicians perform the musical’s key songs. Musical numbers feature Lucy Fisch as Liesl, Jaxon Hunt as Friedrich, Miranda Klein as Louisa, Ray Khalili as Kurt, Sage Luu as Brigitta, Kaylee Lopez as Marta and Erin Koh as Gretl, with music direction by Michael Patrick Wiles. To purchase tickets, call the box office at (510) 845-8542 (extension 351) or visit www. berkeleyplayhouse.org. Showtimes vary.

articles.text: Picnic tables still available, space is limited The San Francisco Symphony performs its annual concert at Stern Grove Festival, a free summer music festival in San Francisco, on Sunday, July 6. The Symphony has performed at the festival every year since its inception 88 years ago. Taimane is renowned for her unique and inventive style of playing the fourstring island instrument and has garnered critical acclaim for her signature stage presence. articles.text: History is like the hall of mirrors. There are many facets. It can be viewed from many directions. The accounts can be compelling, especially when brought on by knaves and phonies. Six of us attended the dress rehearsal of the musical Anastasia at Woodminster Amphitheater in the Oakland hills. Anastasia is a full bodied musical, best described as “a drama played after a tragedy for the purpose of entertainment.” It was all of those things. Musicians of all ages will love this musical, and it will also appeal to historians. Let me tell you why. First of all, Woodminster is a beautiful location now celebrating its 50th anniversary. The productions are fine tuned. A live orchestra is in the pit and the musicians are very proficient. The actual story of Anastasia Romanoff (the youngest daughter of the last czar of Russia) is a fantasy of the highest order. The musical is based on history… in part factual, in part fantasy and in part false history. There are imposters everywhere. The plot has many sub plots. It is almost impossible to tell where history leaves off and fantasy begins. That is the very nature of the true story of Anastasia. Dramatically speaking, this musical is worth seeing. All of the history is explained in dialogues and musically. When the singers perform their arias, the story comes together quite clearly. All of the leading characters have excellent voices and the staging is beautiful. Drama came at the appropriate time and was often riveting. In addition, there is a fabulous ballet scene. Unfortunately, there were no printed programs so I am not able to provide the names of the performers. Nevertheless, Anastasia the musical will appeal to historians and music lovers. My only suggestion is that this Russian story should have had some Russian-sounding music. articles.text: Fried Green Tomatoes is based on the 1987 novel Fried Green Tomatoes at the Whistle Stop Café, written by Fannie Flagg. The film is extraordinary, filled with humor, wonderful portrayals, Oscar nominated, a kaleidoscope of wonderful characters, each giving outstanding performances. The narrative is set in real time Alabama, and opens with Evelyn Couch (Kathy Bates) and her husband, Ed (Gailard Sartain), visiting his aunt at a nearby nursing home. Banished from the visit by Ed’s very cranky aunt, Evelyn goes to the waiting room where she meets an elderly woman seated alone on a sofa. Happy for the company, she introduces herself as Ninny Threadgoode (Jessica Tandy). Small talk quickly evaporates and Ninny begins to share stories from her past, a series of vignettes set in a whisper of a place called Whistle Stop and a café of the same name. She begins telling Evelyn about a young girl named Idgie (later played by an older Mary Stuart Masterson), willful, best described as a Tomboy. It’s at this point that the film cuts to Alabama in the early 1920s. The tale, told by Ninny, initially in the form of introductory voice-over, immediately captures Evelyn’s imagination, and so the audience is introduced to a young Idgie and a slightly older, very feminine Ruth Jamison (Mary Louise Parker), a family relative. Though this brief tale ends in a heartbreaking tragedy, Evelyn, expecting to be rejected by Ed’s aunt, returns to the same waiting room and once again finds Ninny there, alone. And so the soulful story of Idgie and Ruth continues, two women who eventually share a deep bond, and together run the Whistle Stop Café. What the narrative does at this point is weave two stories together: the first involves Evelyn who is attempting to improve her marriage with Ed while acquiring a budding sense of empowerment. She finds inspiration from Ninny and the close relationship that existed between Idgie and Ruth. The audience is reminded that rural Alabama in the 1920s was plagued by a malignant racism. Yet, at the Whistle Stop Café there was a prevailing color-blindness and an abiding humanity, made evident through the remarkable and pivotal performances by cicely Tyson as Sipsy and Stan Shaw as Big George who both worked at the café. Fried Green Tomatoes is a funny, moving story, rich in characters, and is, as well, an intriguing mystery, one that is not answered until the final scenes of this marvelous movie that deftly winds through the past and present. As an aside, Jessica Tandy did win a Best Supporting Actress Oscar for her role as Ninny Threadgoode. She is superb. As well the film won a BAFTA award and three Golden Globe Awards. Fried Green Tomatoes. Directed by John Avnet. Starring Kathy Bates, Jessica Tandy, Mary Stuart Masterson, Mary Louise Parker. 2 hrs., 10 min. PG-13. Released in 1991. articles.text: A scene from Studio Ghibli’s Grave of Fireflies Grave of Fireflies is a mustsee if you have been captured by the extraordinary animation and storytelling that has come to define Studio Ghibli. It is, without hesitation, an achingly beautiful film that transcends all expectations. However know that its story is profoundly sad and emotive, bordering on the traumatic. Because it is animated, and its two main characters are children, it is easy to assume that its subject matter will reflect the fanciful innocence associated with the animé genre. But while this narrative is, to be sure, an allegory of sorts, it also challenges our assumptions about animation. Grave of Fireflies is set in Kobe, Japan. The year is 1945, and WWII is coming to a close, despite the unwillingness of the Japanese to stand down. Told in a long flashback, the tale focuses on a 14-year-old boy named Seita (J. Robert Spencer) and his 5-year-old sister, Setsuko (Rhoda Chrosite). Orphaned by allied fire-bombings, they go to live with their aunt (Amy Jones) whose initial charitable response to the children turns surprisingly bitter until, finally, Seita decides that they must leave. The two find a cave in the hills and for a brief time all is well. But before long malnutrition stalks them. Seita is beaten while looking for food and Setsuko falls ill. Their struggle is the struggle of the vulnerable who must confront events not of their making and the arc of the story is wrenchingly inevitable. articles.text: Lightyear is a kid-friendly, action-adventure spin-off from Disney-Pixar’s Toy Story. And parents might consider the following: if your little guys have not been introduced to the Toy Story franchise, well, start there before heading on to Lightyear. Here is some backstory: in 1995, the year that the first Toy Story was released, it began with Andy, a boy who had a bevy of plastic toy-figures in his room. Buzz Lightyear was not one of them. What happened was that Andy went to the movies and watched a sci-fi action adventure film starring Buzz Lightyear, and he was smitten. Loved the character, which became an action figure. For Christmas, of course, under the tree was Buzz What Lightyear is not is a film about how Buzz ends up in Andy’s room, joining the gang of figures that come to life, so to speak. Instead, Lightyear is the film that captured Andy’s imagination. In other words, it’s sort of an origin tale that stands alone and is only referenced in Toy Story. So far so good? The question then begged is, what was there about this animated story that so captured Andy’s imagination? First, the tale unfolds with Buzz (Chris Evans), a charismatic, all-American, lantern-jawed space ranger and a crew of hundreds on board a Star Trek-like deep space star ship, akin to the iconic EnterA scene from Disney-Pixar animation’s Lightyear prise. In command is Alisha Hawthorne (Uzo Aduba). The ship is 4.2 million light years from Earth on a deep space mission, all have been in deep hibernation. Awakened, hey decide to explore an unfamiliar planet named T’Kani Prime. Of course, stuff happens that provides excitement. The planet has breathable air; however the ship is damaged on landing, plus there are hostile, voracious insect-like creatures that threaten the crew. What allows the ship to travel at warp speed is a hyperspeed crystal that is also in need of repair. Of course, Buzz is the obvious choice to be the test pilot. This is when time travel comes into play and the story does get a bit convoluted. Buzz takes the crystal out for a very short test; however, when he returns he discovers that four years have passed on the planet. There’s also an evil emperor, Zurg (James Brolin), who threatens the new colony now established on T’Kani Prime. He has an army of robotic soldiers. There is also a scene-stealing robotic cat named Sox (Peter Sohn) who is Buzz’s close companion. Think of the critter as Buzz’s feline wingman and advisor. It’s all wonderfully animated, filled with lots of action and adventure, and a great introduction to Buzz Lightyear, a swaggering daredevil, dedicated to the mission no matter the breathtaking risk Lightyear. Carter With school out for summer, last Wednesday the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesday group enjoyed a guided walk through the Piedmont High School campus. Forty-one walkers (plus two K-9 best friends) gathered at the Exedra to explore notable features and local history. Before the walk, the group learned about the origins of Piedmont High. In 1916, land developer Frank C. Havens faced financial ruin. A onetime real estate speculator, he returned to California with little left, attempting to sell land to settle debts. Piedmont Park was heavily mortgaged, and Havens was unable to pay interest or principal. He auctioned his art collection and hoped to sell the parkland. The Piedmont School Board wanted 13 acres for a new high school and athletic field, but Havens refused to split the 27-acre parcel. The City also wanted to preserve the park but lacked funds. In November 1916, voters rejected a measure to purchase the remaining land. Havens died in 1918. In 1921, philanthropist Wallace Alexander stepped in. He and other donors bought 14 acres on the condition the City would later reimburse them. The deal allowed the School District to purchase its desired 13 acres. The next year, voters approved a bond to repay Alexander and his partners, securing the entire 27 acres. The walkers followed a path behind the Exedra to the high school’s rear entrance and continued past the student center and library, where more history was shared. Construction of Piedmont High began in 1921, designed by architect William Weeks. The reinforced concrete structure with terra cotta trim included an auditorium, two classroom wings, and separate science and cooking labs. Piedmont Junior High and the athletic field were added in 1924, with further additions in 1937 and 1939. In 1974, the original building was declared unsafe under new earthquake laws and demolished—though the process was slow due to the building’s sturdy construction. Three new classroom buildings and a gym replaced it, while the original library, quad, and administration buildings were preserved. That era’s “back-to-nature” wooden buildings, popular in the 1970s, were later deemed earthquake unsafe and also removed. With the passage of Measure H1, voters approved $56 million in bonds for safe, modern facilities. A new STEAM building and theater opened in fall 2021. The walkers also heard that Piedmont High was the last school in California to drop its enforced dress code, which required girls to wear middy blouses and pleated skirts until the early 1960s. Alumna Sherry Jacobs remembered the uniform’s upside—it made dressing for school simple. The group made a brief stop at the under-construction aquatics center, where fresh concrete had been poured but swimming likely won’t resume this summer. They continued past Millennium High, Binks Rawlings Gym, and Piedmont Middle School, then down “PE Hill” to the locker rooms and Witter Field. At Witter Field, the group paused at the monument to Jean C. Witter Jr., a 1940s PHS football captain and Cal player who died in WWII aboard the USS San Francisco. The field was named for him in 1948. The scoreboard also honors Charles Williams, a 1948 team member. Nearby, walkers passed Humphries Diamond, named for longtime teacher and coach Mike Humphries, who led PHS baseball for 33 years and freshman football for 43. Emerging on lower El Cerrito Avenue, the group climbed Jerome Avenue, detoured through Keefer Court to admire a unique cactus garden and Santa Fe– inspired front yards, and posed for a group photo. The final stretch took them across Oakland Avenue and up Latham Street—famously the only “street” in Piedmont—then on to Cambridge Way, Ricardo Avenue, and Blair Avenue. They finished the loop via Carmel Avenue and Bonita Vista back to the Exedra. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 AM. articles.text: As our country navigates a multitude of challenges, service dogs are bringing hope and relief to many struggling to cope with the stress of everyday life. Protected by federal law under the Americans With Disabilities Act, these highly trained animals are more than just pets – they’re lifesavers. Service dogs are trained to actively mitigate an individual’s disability. These specially trained canines provide critical support to individuals struggling with a wide range of disabilities, both visible and invisible. Curious how service dogs improve their owners’ lives every day? Musubi, a Miniature Golden Doodle, alerts his owner to the sound of the smoke alarm, ensuring her safety despite her hearing loss. Other trained service dogs, like the Great Dane Scooter, provide mobility assistance in the form of balance support and fall recovery to their owners. And still more, like June and Nala, are currently in training to remind their owner to take medication or alert them to oncoming panic attacks. Facility dogs, while not protected by federal law, also make a difference in the lives of many. These dogs partner with working professionals to serve their clients, often going into schools, healthcare centers, and even family court. Dogs like Missy, the Australian Shepherd, partner with a therapist and are trained to help decrease anxiety in children. Stinson, a Labradoodle, spends time in schools as a reading dog to help children build confidence and improve their reading skills. articles.text: Order of the Arrow is an honor society within Scouting America to promote cheerful service above self. It recognizes Scouts who best exemplify and live by the Scout oath, law, motto and slogan. Piedmont’s lodge is called Hungteetsepoppi, meaning ‘bird with red head’, a reference to the bird that represents our lodge. Year round the lodge helps the Piedmont Scout Council with various aspects of Piedmont scouting, such as the Cub Scout Webeloree, where we prepare dinner and a campfire on the first night. We also help set up and take down the Tree Lot at the end of the season. In addition, the OA participates in larger events, such as the section-wide Conclave, a gathering of multiple lodges from the area. Similar to Camporee, Conclave is usually a larger event and features master classes on certain aspects of the OA, such as ceremonies and membership retention. Events also take place at the regional and national level, such as the National Leadership Seminar and exclusive experiences at the four national high adventure bases. On June 8th, our lodge celebrated a successful year of leadership, community service, and new members with a lodge-wide barbecue, and a brotherhood ceremony. Brotherhood is recognition you receive after being an active member of the lodge for six months, and show a strong understanding of the ideals of the OA. It’s not a rank to progress through, but rather an indicator of your commitment to the highest ideals of Scouting The celebration was followed by a barbeque before beginning the elections for the upcoming year. One unique aspect of the OA is that it’s fully youth led. While Scouting has a large amount of youth input and leadership, the OA is only restrained by what the youth leaders can put into place and organize. Everything, down to the elections of lodge officers are entirely youth run. Vice Chief of Program Caleb Canada (left), Vice Chief of Membership Sean McKee, Lodge Chief Theo Ferguson, and Vice Chief of Communication Samantha Pell For me, this is a testament to the truest displays of character, and an excellent foundation for lifelong connections and valuable lessons on leadership. To quote our National Chief, Samuel Crowder’s Chiefly Thoughts “...such a simple display of his appreciation and love for his friends, but it spoke volumes on what he truly enjoyed, and I would argue most love about the Order of the Arrow: the people”. The people are what truly make the OA an enjoyable and formative experience, one that is certainly worth being a part of. If you are an active Scouter in Piedmont and interested in joining the Order of the Arrow, please reach out to your Scoutmaster for additional information. articles.text: The Piedmont Seniors recently visited the historic Elliston Winery in Sunol, where they toured the estate and enjoyed an elegant tea featuring open-faced sandwiches, scones, and decadent desserts. Tucked away in the Sunol hills, Elliston Vineyards offers a picturesque setting for outdoor tea or special events. Its lush grounds, historic stone mansion, and secluded Terrace Room create a memorable backdrop for any occasion. The Elliston estate was established by Henry Hiram Ellis, who came to California in 1849 during the Gold Rush. He later served as San Francisco’s last elected chief of police from 1875 to 1877, and Ellis Street was named in his honor. In 1885, Ellis purchased a scenic, oak-studded property in Sunol for his retirement. Between 1885 and 1890, he built Elliston—a 17-room, three-story neo-Romanesque mansion constructed with 32-inch-thick blue sandstone walls quarried nearby in Niles Canyon. The estate is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Following their tea, the Seniors headed to Niles, where they strolled through the Town Plaza, browsed antique shops, and enjoyed ice cream from a local parlor. With more than 40 antique and specialty stores, the area offers plenty of unique finds. Niles also boasts a rich history. Established in the 1850s, it served as a key junction for Southern Pacific Railroad lines connecting Oakland, San Jose, and points south. It once housed the state’s largest rose plantation and later became a hub for early filmmaking. In 1912, Essanay Studios brought national attention to Niles. Led by Bronco Billy Anderson, the studio filmed silent-era classics with stars like Charlie Chaplin, Wallace Beery, and Ben Turpin. Many westerns were shot in Niles Canyon and on the town’s main streets. Strolling through the neighborhood, the Piedmont Seniors appreciated Niles’ historic charm, friendly shops, and relaxed, welcoming vibe. It was, all in all, a peaceful and thoroughly enjoyable day. articles.text: Ever wished you could bring a slice of nature indoors but worried about the commitment of a full-fledged houseplant? Terrariums offer the perfect solution. These miniature ecosystems housed in glass containers are a captivating display of greenery that requires minimal care. Choosing the perfect container: Select a clear glass container to allow plenty of sunlight to reach your plants. Bowls, apothecary jars or even recycled fish tanks with wide openings are all great options. Choose a container that’s large enough to comfortably fit the drainage layers, potting mix and your plants at their mature size. Picking the perfect plants: When choosing plants, consider both their mature size and the limitations of your container. Here are some low-maintenance options that thrive in drier environments: • Pincushion cactus • Air plants • Hens and chicks • Button fern Pro tip: Select plants with similar light and watering needs to ensure a harmonious environment within your terrarium. Building a foundation for success: Terrariums don’t have drainage holes, making it extra important to create a well-draining base to prevent root rot. Drainage layer: • Add a layer of coarse gravel, sea glass or beach stones to the bottom of your container. A good foundation made up of different layers of material is essential for the well being of the terrarium. Succulents, air plants, cacti and ferns work great in open terrariums. Barrier layer: • Next, add a quarter- to halfinch layer of activated charcoal on top of the gravel. This will help prevent fungus growth. • Then, cover the stones and charcoal with a layer of sphagnum moss. This will prevent the potting soil from mixing in with the drainage layers. (Do not use peat moss for this layer.) Soil layer: • Add sterile potting mix on top of the moss. The soil should be formulated for the plants you’ve picked, such as a cactus and succulent mix. Planting and design: Here’s where you can unleash your creativity. Before planting, take some time to design the layout of your terrarium. Carefully remove your plants from their pots, loosen the roots and gently brush away any excess dirt. Play with the arrangement to create a visually interesting composition. Once you’re happy with the layout, use a spoon or your fingers to carefully plant each one in your terrarium. Fill in any gaps with moss for a natural, finished look. Caring for your terrarium: Light: Terrariums prefer bright, indirect sunlight. Avoid direct sunlight, which can scorch your plants. Rotate your terrarium occasionally for even growth. Watering: Less is more when it comes to watering your terrarium. Use a spray bottle or tablespoon to add water sparingly when the soil is dry. Upkeep: Remove yellowing or dead plants right away. Occasionally wipe down the glass with damp newspaper or a lint-free cloth. Adding your personal touch: Finally, it’s time to decorate. Add elements like small rocks, figurines or colorful gravel to personalize your miniature world. Enjoy your thriving little world! Debbi DiMaggio Debbi. He ended the season as the Southern California Intercollegiate Athletic Conference Player of the Year. Wagener finished the year with a team-leading 73 goals, to go along with 16 assists. For Scout skills, a tent-pitching competition saw Dens racing to be the fastest to set up their tent and a class on basic first aid. At the cooking station, campers enjoyed the chef’s relay race and solar-cooked s’mores. The STEM station included bottle rockets using only air and water, as well as aluminum foil boats. One camper’s boat held a record 200 pennies before sinking. Campers played plenty of games in between the activities, like “Duck Duck Goose” and “Captain’s Coming,” which has campers pretending to look out of a crow’s nest, searching for a man overboard, and dining in a ship’s mess hall. The Day Camp presents leadership opportunities for older Scouts. This year’s camp had scout volunteers of various ranks from Piedmont’s five troops. As per tradition, the camp culminated in its much-anticipated egg drop contest, where Scouts put their creative minds to the test by finding the best way to drop a raw egg from a height of seven stories without the egg breaking. Members of the Piedmont Fire Department assisted by dropping the eggs, one by one, in homemade protective enclosures from the engine’s 75-foot extension ladder. The contest is unique in that Scouts are given very few limitations on how to achieve their goal. The container’s dimension must measure less than 8” x 8” x 8”, the egg must be raw, and campers may not affix anything to the egg itself. Other than that, anything goes. articles.text: The Piedmont Fire Department invites community members to provide feedback on the June 14 community wildfire evacuation exercise. Whether residents participated in the practical exercise for the Blair/Scenic/Alta neighborhood, completed the at-home family exercise, or did not participate in either, the City wants to know: • If you received the “THIS IS A DRILL” AC Alert notification on Saturday morning • How well the activity helped you think through your own evacuation planning • What, if any, actions the exercise prompted you to take • What was confusing or didn’t work well • What types of preparedness programs, resources, or activities you would like to see in the future The feedback survey is available online at piedmont.ca.gov/WildfireSurvey. At-Home activity still available The at-home evacuation activity that was developed for the June 14 exercise will remain available on the City’s website at piedmont.ca.gov/wildfiredrill. The Fire Department encourages those who were not able to participate this weekend to plan a time to complete the exercise soon. The at-home activity is designed for families, housemates, or neighbors to complete together. A short video guides residents through a realistic, local wildfire scenario based on conditions in Piedmont. It also includes discussion prompts and a printable worksheet to help households plan and reflect. Participants should plan about 30 to 45 minutes to complete the exercise. Visit piedmont.ca.gov/wildfire for more information and resources on preparing for wildfires, including packing a go bag, preparing yards for fire season, and hardening homes against wildfires.
